debugCase.t: The model reasoned poorly and just picked the wrong policy from context it had access to
debugCase.why: The model's reasoning isn't actually the failure here, it answered fluently and confidently FROM the context it was given, that's exactly what a model does with retrieved text. The evidence points upstream, to what got retrieved in the first place.

debugCase.t: A stale, superseded document (support-faq-2023.md) was retrieved above the relevance threshold and blended into the answer, with no recency or supersession signal to exclude it
debugCase.why: Look at the evidence: chunk [3] is explicitly marked "superseded by pricing.md in 2024" in its own metadata, yet it still cleared the 0.35 threshold and made it into context, because cosine similarity only measures semantic closeness to the query, it has no idea one document replaced another. The model's answer ("email support, up to two weeks") matches chunk [3] almost verbatim, while chunk [1], the CURRENT, correct policy, scored higher but got blended with an outdated one instead of overriding it. The fix isn't a bigger model, it's a retrieval-layer signal: filter or down-rank superseded documents before they ever reach the prompt.

debugCase.t: The embedding model doesn't understand subscription cancellation as a concept
debugCase.why: The scores say otherwise, all three chunks scored well above the 0.35 threshold on a query about cancellation, the embeddings clearly captured the topic correctly. The problem isn't topic understanding, it's that relevance and currency are two different properties, and only one of them was checked.

debugCase.t: k was set too high, and a smaller k would have fixed it
debugCase.why: Lowering k to 1 or 2 might accidentally drop the stale chunk here, but that's luck, not a fix, it depends entirely on which chunk happens to score highest on a given query, and would just as easily drop the CORRECT current-policy chunk on a different phrasing. The real gap is that nothing in the system checks whether a retrieved document has been superseded, k doesn't address that at all.
